# ACTIVE: A Dynamic Pareto-Frontier-Based Unified Index for Dual-Vector Query ### ABSTRACT Existing approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) methods generally assume that each entity has a single vector. In many real-world applications, however, an entity is associated with more than one vector, and queries may jointly consider two attributes. With different queries assigning different weights to each attribute, Pareto-frontier-based indices provide an effective solution for dual- vector retrieval by connecting to approximate nearest neighbors under all possible query preferences. However, existing Pareto- frontier-based approaches suffer from substantial inefficiencies in both index construction and dynamic updates, limiting their practical applicability. To address these issues, we propose ACTIVE , a dynamic Pareto- frontier-based DVQ index that supports efficient construction and updates while maintaining high retrieval performance under varying query preferences. It employs angle-constrained active-range computation and connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategies to accelerate node insertion and deletion, respectively. Extensive experiments show that, at comparable (or slightly below) search accuracy, ACTIVE improves insertion throughput by 1.20-1.43\(\times\) over DEG, and deletion throughput by 1.64-2.06\(\times\) over neighbor- reconnection-based repair and by 22.64-39.51\(\times\) over reinsertion- based repair. ### 1 INTRODUCTION Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high- dimensional vectors has been widely adopted in applications such as recommendation systems [12, 34, 42, 43] and information retrieval [4, 33, 55, 65]. In these applications, the unstructured attributes of an entity, such as image, text, or audio, are embedded into vectors, and objects whose vectors are close (similar) to the query vector are retrieved. Traditional ANNS primarily focuses on single-vector retrieval [9, 16, 19, 22, 23, 30, 50, 59], i.e., entities are searched based on only _one_ unstructured (vectorized) attribute. However, many real-world retrieval tasks require jointly considering more than one vectorized attribute [5, 11, 32, 38, 39, 46, 48], with query-specific preferences assigned to each attribute. In this paper, we focus on dual-vector retrieval with exactly two attribute vectors, which is common in applications with complementary modalities, such as image-text of products on e-commerce platforms [20, 48, 61], spatial-textual data of posts on social platforms [11], and video-text of videos on short-video platforms [32, 61]. Given a query with two vectors, the distance between the query and an object is the weighted sum of their distances on the two vectors, where the query-specific preference determines the weight of each attribute distance. As query preferences vary, the distance between the same pair of entities changes accordingly, making efficient and accurate ANN retrieval particularly challenging. Furthermore, real- world datasets are inherently dynamic, with entities continuously being inserted and deleted. Such dynamic updates pose significant challenges to efficient index-based retrieval methods. **Example 1:** In product search on e-commerce platforms, consider two users who upload images of a smartphone and provide textual descriptions, such as "a smartphone with long battery life and excellent photography". The first user aims to retrieve a smartphone that visually resembles the uploaded image, whereas the second user prioritizes the specific performance attribute. Accordingly, the first user assigns a larger weight to the image-vector distance, while the second user assigns a larger weight to the textual- vector distance when computing similarity based on the image and textual embeddings. Even when the two users provide the same phone image and textual description, different preferences can lead to different retrieval results. Meanwhile, vendors continuously update product listings due to inventory changes, ensuring accurate retrieval results for users. This makes the dynamic updating of dual- vector data indispensable. Thus, the DVQ problem requires efficient and accurate retrieval under arbitrary query preferences while also supporting efficient dynamic updates. \(\sqcap\sqcup\) **Motivation.** Existing DVQ approaches [48, 49, 61, 63] mainly build graph-based ANNS indices over dual-vector data to enable efficient retrieval. However, they cannot simultaneously achieve high retrieval accuracy and high update efficiency. In general, these approaches can be divided into two categories. 1)Preference-specific multi-indices. These approaches [48, 49, 63] build single-vector indices by fixing the query preference in advance. A representative solution is multi-index retrieval (MR) [48, 63], which builds a separate index for each attribute vector. Since they assume that object distances are pre-determined, they suffer from limited retrieval quality under arbitrary query preferences, as shown in Figure 1a.

<u>_2) Preference-agnostic unified indices_</u>. Unlike existing single-vector indices \[16, 22, 30\] that select similar vectors of each node as their neighbors, this approach \[61\] connects approximate nearest neighbors across all possible query preferences, ensuring that varying query preferences can be accommodated during search. To achieve this, approximate Pareto frontiers are utilized as the neighbors since they remain competitive under diverse preference settings, thereby enabling the selected neighbors to cover varying query preferences. As a result, Pareto-frontier-based indices provide a more suitable foundation for query-dependent similarity search in DVQ. However, existing unified indices do not support efficient dynamic updates because repairing Pareto frontiers is more complex than repairing neighbors in single-vector indices \[28, 47, 62\].

**Our goal**. In this work, we aim to design a dynamic Pareto-frontier- based DVQ index that supports efficient construction and updates while maintaining high retrieval performance.

**Challenges**. Designing a preference-agnostic unified index is challenging for two main reasons.

<u>_1) Expensive Edge Active-Range Computation in Construction_</u>. Pareto-frontier-based indices \[61\] select neighbors to cover different query preferences, but not every selected edge is useful under every preference. Thus, each edge needs to precompute its active ranges of the preference, allowing it to be traversed only when needed and avoiding redundant distance computations. Employing Relative Neighborhood Graph (RNG) pruning \[61\] enables the computation of such active ranges, however, its expensive time complexity introduces substantial additional computational overhead. Therefore, designing an efficient active-range computation method remains challenging.

<u>_2) Inefficient Approximate Pareto Frontier Repair in Update_</u>. In Pareto-frontier-based indices, repairing the Pareto-frontier neighbors of affected nodes (i.e., in-neighbors of deleted nodes) after deletions is critical to preserving graph connectivity. Reinsertion- based global repair strategies \[2, 30, 60\] rediscover the neighbors of affected nodes by traversing from entry nodes, causing many distance computations and high update overhead. However, directly applying single-vector local repair strategies \[47, 62\] to Pareto- frontier-based DVQ indices is ineffective, as validated in Figure 1b and 1c, since they cannot guarantee that Pareto frontiers can be identified within the local neighborhood of DVQ indices. Therefore, designing an efficient repair strategy for approximate Pareto frontiers while maintaining high retrieval accuracy remains challenging.

**ACTIVE**. The above challenges cannot be directly addressed by existing techniques. Starting from these application-level challenges, we propose ACTIVE , a `dynAmiC` Pareto-fronTier-based unIfied `DVQ` indEx that supports dynamic updates while maintaining high retrieval quality under arbitrary query preferences. ACTIVE is built upon two techniques.

To accelerate index construction, we introduce the Pareto angle and develop an `angle-constrained active range` computation algorithm, ACAR, based on the locality distribution of Pareto angles. In ACAR, each neighbor is compared only with other neighbors that satisfy the angle constraint under the triangle inequality. By restricting unnecessary comparisons, ACAR reduces construction overhead while preserving effective navigation quality of the DVQ index across diverse query preferences.

For efficient updates, we observe a high overlap between the original neighbors and the repaired neighbors of affected nodes and introduce CA-PFR, a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategy that locally repairs approximate Pareto frontiers. We provide three methods, namely historical-Pareto-frontier, affected- layer, and multi-layer repair, according to the severity of connectivity degradation of affected nodes. This allows us to restore the connectivity of the graph without full re-insertion, significantly reducing distance computations and improving update throughput.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are:<tbc>

\(\bullet\) An observation of Pareto-angle locality motivates an angle- constrained active range computation algorithm, which accelerates active range computation (§ 4).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) An observation of high overlap between original and repaired neighbors of affected nodes motivates an incremental repair method. We propose a connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair strategy, which locally repairs approximate Pareto frontiers according to the severity of connectivity degradation (§ 5).<tbc>

\(\bullet\) Extensive experiments on diverse datasets show that ACTIVE achieves higher update throughput than state-of-the-art baselines while maintaining a competitive trade-off between query accuracy and efficiency (§ 6).

## 2 BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION

In this section, we first define the Dual-Vector Query (DVQ) problem and review Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index construction as well as update methods for single-vector graph-based indices. We then analyze their drawbacks and present the motivation of this work.

### 2.1 Dual-Vector Query

Let _O_={_o_<sub>0</sub>_,o_<sub>1</sub>_,...,o_<sub>_N_-1</sub>} denote a dataset of _N_ objects, where each object \(o_i\in O\) is represented by two feature vectors: (1) \(o_i.x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}\), a _d<sub>x</sub>_-dimensional vector capturing one attribute, and (2) \(o_i.y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}\), a _d<sub>y</sub>_-dimensional vector capturing another attribute.

**Dual-Vector Query (DVQ)**. Given a query \(q=\langle x,y,\alpha,k\rangle\), where \(q.x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}\) and \(q.y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}\) are the query vectors, \(q.\alpha\in[0,1]\) is a weighting parameter provided by upstream applications to quantify user preferences, and _q.k_ is the number of objects to retrieve. Ideally, DVQ aims to retrieve the exact top-_k_ nearest objects \(R_{exact}\subset O\) for a query _q_, such that \(\forall e\in R_{exact},\forall o\in O\backslash R_{exact}\), we have \(\text{Dist}(q,e)\le\text{Dist}(q,o)\), where the distance \[61\] between _q_ and an object _o_ is defined as:

\(\text{Dist}(q,o)=q.\alpha\cdot\delta_x(q,o)+(1-q.\alpha)\cdot\delta_y(q,o),\) (1)

where \(\delta_x(q,o)=\frac{\|q.x-o.x\|_2}{x_\text{max}}\) and \(\delta_y(q,o)=\frac{\|q.y-o.y\|_2}{y_\text{max}}\) are the normalized distances for each vector. A larger \(\alpha\) means the user prefers the _x_-attribute, while a smaller \(\alpha\) means the user prefers the _y_-attribute. In real applications, \(\alpha\) can be learned and tuned based on the user’s query history and the entities ultimately selected.

However, the retrieval of _R<sub>exact</sub>_ requires exhaustive search over the entire dataset, which becomes computationally expensive and incurs high search latency [21]. To address this, DVQ in practice retrieves _k_ approximate nearest results _R<sub>DVQ</sub>_, achieving a trade- off between retrieval accuracy and search efficiency [21, 61]. To quantify the quality of the approximate results _R<sub>DVQ</sub>_, recall [26, 51] is commonly used, defined as \(Recall@k=\frac{|R_{DVQ}\cap R_{exact}|}{k}\) , where _R<sub>exact</sub>_ is the ground-truth set of the _k_ closest objects to _q_. The goal of DVQ is to maximize recall while retrieving results efficiently.

## 2.2 Pareto-Frontier-Based Index Construction

Due to diverse query \(\alpha\) in DVQ, Pareto-frontier-based indices select the Pareto frontiers of each node as its out-neighbors, which can nearly cover the approximate nearest neighbors for all possible \(\alpha\).

**Pareto Frontier** [29]. The construction of Pareto-frontier-based indices can be viewed as finding the Pareto frontier for each node. Given a node \(v\in V\) for which we aim to find its neighbors, each candidate node \(p\in V\backslash\{v\}\) induces a distance pair relative to _v_, \((\delta_x(v,p),\delta_y(v,p))\). For any \(p,q\in V\backslash\{v\}\), we say that _p dominates q_, denoted by \(p\prec q\), if and only if (1) \(\forall i\in\{x,y\},\delta_i(v,p)\le\delta_i(v,q)\), and (2) \(\exists j\in\{x,y\},\delta_j(v,p)<\delta_j(v,q)\). The Pareto frontier of _v_ is defined as \(PF_v\subseteq V\backslash\{v\}\), where \(\forall p\in PF_v\), \(\nexists q\in V\backslash\{v\},q\prec p\), i.e., the neighbors of _v_ in _PF<sub>v</sub>_ cannot be dominated by any node.

**Multi-layer Pareto Frontiers**. In Pareto-frontier-based indices, only using the Pareto frontier of each node as its out-neighbors leads to an extremely sparse graph index. This is because, in a dataset with millions of objects, the size of the Pareto frontier is typically small (e.g., the average size is 8.26 on CC3M) , while hundreds of candidate nodes are usually required to select as the final out-neighbors. To address this, the multi-layer Pareto frontiers \(\{PF_v^1,\dots,PF_v^l\}\) are selected as the candidate out-neighbors of each node _v_, where _l_ is the number of layers bounded by the candidate pool size _ef<sub>construct</sub>_, as shown in Figure 2b. Neighbors in the first layer correspond to the global Pareto frontier. Each subsequent layer is recursively constructed by removing the current Pareto frontier and extracting a new Pareto frontier from the remaining candidates, referred to as FindPF [7].

**Approximate Pareto Frontier Search**. However, the construction of exact multi-layer Pareto frontiers is computationally expensive, as it requires computing distances to all other nodes in the dataset for each node. Therefore, approximate Pareto frontiers are typically used as candidate neighbors for each node, which are constructed using the Greedy Pareto Frontier Search (GPS) to expand candidate neighbors layer by layer (see Algorithm 1). Specifically, GPS iteratively expands unexplored nodes in the lowest layer of Pareto frontiers containing them until no unexplored nodes remain. Finally, the candidate set C is selected as the approximate Pareto frontier.

**Active Range (AR) Computation**. Since the out-neighbors of each node cover the nearest neighbors under varying query<tbc>

<tbc>preferences, a significant portion of the outgoing edges need not be traversed for a given \(\alpha\) value. To accelerate query processing, we assign preference intervals (i.e., _active ranges_) to each edge, enabling the system to selectively traverse only the edges whose active ranges include the query \(\alpha\). However, computing the active ranges of each edge is difficult [61]. DEG adopts an RNG-inspired pruning strategy similar to those used in single-vector graph indices. Specifically, for each candidate neighbor in C corresponding to an outgoing edge, it evaluates the distance to every other candidate neighbor and computes an interval of the parameter \(\alpha\) over which the edge becomes the longest edge in the corresponding triangle configuration. The active range is then obtained by excluding all such intervals from the complete parameter domain [0,1]. This method requires comparing each neighbor of a node with all retained neighbors to determine its active ranges, resulting in a time complexity of \(O(R\cdot|\mathcal{C}|)\), where _R_ is the maximum out-degree.

**Summary**. Existing Pareto-frontier-based DVQ index construction methods still face performance challenges, as the active range computation introduces substantial computational overhead.

## 2.3 Pareto-Frontier-Based Index Updates

In real-world scenarios, timely updates of indices are essential for search accuracy. Although no specialized DVQ index has yet been proposed to efficiently support dynamic updates, especially for node deletions, existing update techniques for single-vector graph- based indices are already well-established [2, 47, 60, 62]. Next, we review representative update methods in existing single-vector graph-based indices. The insertion procedure can follow the same logic as the construction process. Therefore, we focus our discussion on the deletion case.

Existing repair strategies can be broadly classified into the following two categories: 1) _Reinsertion-Based Repair (RBR)_ methods [2, 30, 60] treat affected nodes as newly inserted nodes and reinsert them to reconstruct their out-neighbors. Although these methods can maintain high index quality, the global search incurs significant computational overhead. 2) _Neighbor-Reconnection- Based Repair (NRBR)_ methods [47, 62] restore graph connectivity through local reconnections, based on the intuition that neighbors of neighbors are likely to remain close to the affected node. Compared with RBR, NRBR may degrade index quality while achieving higher update throughput. However, in Pareto-frontier-based DVQ indices, these NRBR methods cannot guarantee that the neighbors of a node’s neighbors belong to its Pareto frontiers, making it difficult to maintain high retrieval accuracy.

**Summary**. Update strategies for single-vector graph indices provide useful insights for DVQ index updates. For instance, the<tbc>

<tbc>insertion operation can largely reuse techniques from incremental construction. Nevertheless, efficient updates for DVQ indices remain challenging. In particular, designing an efficient deletion repair strategy that preserves high index quality remains challenging.

**Limitations.** Based on the analysis in Section 2.2 and 2.3, existing Pareto-frontier-based DVQ indices suffer from inefficient index construction and substantial update overhead.

## 3 OVERVIEW

To overcome the above limitations, we design ACTIVE , as shown in Figure 3. To accelerate index construction, 1) we introduce an _angle-constrained active range computation_ (§4) strategy that avoids comparing each candidate neighbor against all retained neighbors by leveraging angular constraints. To accelerate index updates, 2) we propose a _connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair_ (§5) strategy that locally repairs the approximate Pareto frontiers of affected nodes according to the severity of their connectivity degradation. Furthermore, we incorporate _asynchronous reverse graph maintenance_ to efficiently locate the affected nodes (§5.2).

<u>_Index Construction_</u>. ACTIVE employs an incremental construction strategy for each object in the dataset. Specifically, when constructing the out-neighbors of node _v_, the candidate set C is obtained by performing greedy Pareto frontier search over the current index. Subsequently, ACTIVE computes the active ranges of nodes in C using the proposed ACAR and selects the top-_R_ unpruned neighbors in lower layers of Pareto-frontiers as the final out-neighbors _N_<sub>out</sub>(_v_). Finally, for each \(v'\in N_\mathrm{out}(v)\), a reverse edge \((v',v)\) is added to guarantee reachability of _v_ during subsequent searches.

<u>_Index Update_</u>. For insertion, ACTIVE adopts the incremental construction approach to add new nodes into the graph index. For deletion, ACTIVE first leverages reverse graph topology to quickly locate the affected nodes. Then, ACTIVE adaptively repairs the affected nodes with three methods, namely historical-Pareto-frontier repair, affected-layer repair, and multi-layer repair, according to the severity of connectivity degradation for each affected node. Finally, ACTIVE computes the active ranges of the candidate neighbors for each affected node and selects the resulting final neighbors.

<u>_Dual-Vector Query_</u>. For a given dual-vector query _q_ and a query preference \(\alpha\), ACTIVE performs the greedy search based on the distance function (i.e., Eq.1) to obtain the top-_k_ approximate nearest neighbors. Specifically, ACTIVE maintains a candidate queue _Q<sub>c</sub>_ and a result queue _Q<sub>r</sub>_, where _Q<sub>c</sub>_ contains the visited but not expanded nodes while _Q<sub>r</sub>_ contains the expanded nodes, both ordered by their distances to the query. At each iteration, the<tbc>

<tbc>first not expanded node \(Q_c^\mathrm{t}\) in _Q<sub>c</sub>_ is selected for expansion, i.e., its out-neighbors whose active ranges contain \(\alpha\) are inserted into _Q<sub>c</sub>_. The expanded node is then inserted into _Q<sub>r</sub>_. During the search, |_Q<sub>r</sub>_| is bounded by _ef_search. The search terminates when \(\mathrm{Dist}(q,Q_c^\mathrm{t})>\mathrm{Dist}(q,Q_r^\mathrm{b})\), where\(Q_r^\mathrm{b}\) is the last node in _Q<sub>r</sub>_.

## 4 ANGLE-CONSTRAINED ACTIVE RANGE COMPUTATION

The workflow reveals that active range (AR) computation is invoked during both index construction and updates. This additional overhead substantially degrades both construction and update efficiency. To reduce this cost, we exploit the visited characteristics of Pareto- frontier-based neighbors and introduce an angle-constrained AR computation algorithm that improves computational efficiency.

### 4.1 Pareto Angle

The existing AR computation algorithm \[61\] computes the active ranges of the candidate set C of a node in a nested-loop manner. The **forward traversal order** of C follows a **two-level sorting scheme**: nodes are first ordered by the layer of the Pareto frontiers in ascending order and then sorted within each layer _PF_ by their distance to _v_ along a given dimension (e.g., \(\delta_x(v,\cdot)\)). Specifically, when processing node _v_, DEG sequentially traverses its out-neighbors (_a,b,c,d,e,f,..._) to compute their active ranges, following a two- level order: from lower to higher Pareto-frontier layers (i.e., layer 1 to _l_), and within each layer in ascending order of \(\delta_x(v,\cdot)\), i.e., from node _a_ to _e_ as illustrated in Figure 4. When traversing node _f_, DEG compares it against all previously retained nodes, i.e., _a-e_. However, this strategy performs redundant comparisons for each candidate neighbor. For _f_, it is unnecessary to compare _f_ with _e_, since _f_ is close to the \(\delta_y(v,\cdot)\) axis while _e_ lies closer to the \(\delta_x(v,\cdot)\) axis, making it highly unlikely that they will be simultaneously retrieved during query processing. Before introducing our AC computation method, we first introduce Pareto Angle.

Definition 1 (Pareto Angle (\(\phi\))). _Given a node v and its out- neighbor c, the Pareto angle_ \(\phi(v,c)\) _is defined in the 2D space induced by_ \((\delta_x(v,c),\delta_y(v,c))\)_. We define_

\(\phi(v,c)=\mathrm{arccos}\left(\frac{(\delta_x(v,c),\delta_y(v,c))\cdot(0,1)}{\sqrt{\delta_x(v,c)^2+\delta_y(v,c)^2}}\right),\) (2)

_where_ \(\phi(v,c)\) _denotes the angle between the vector_ \(\left(\delta_x(v,c),\delta_y(v,c)\right)\) _and the positive_ \(\delta_y(v,\cdot)\)_-axis. The value of_ \(\phi(v,c)\) _lies in_ \([0,\pi/2]\).

From Figure 5, we make the following key observation: _Pareto-Angle Locality_. Retrieved nodes exhibit strong locality in the Pareto angle space, where high-frequency Pareto angle regions form contiguous intervals. For instance, when \(\alpha=0.1\), nodes with higher retrieval frequency are mainly distributed in the range of \(cos(\phi)\in[0.2,0.4]\). **Intuition.** Based on the observation, it is unnecessary for each neighbor to be compared against all other neighbors when computing its active range. Instead, comparisons should be restricted to neighbors with small differences in Pareto angle values. This is because such neighbors are more likely to be jointly retrieved under a given preference parameter \(\alpha\), and hence jointly participate in forming triangles with the target node during graph traversal. ## 4.2 Active Range Computation Based on Pareto Angle Difference Based on the above intuition, we propose an angle-constrained active range computation algorithm, _ACAR_, which leverages the Pareto angle constraint to avoid unnecessary distance computations. The core idea of ACAR is that, for any two candidate neighbors _e_ and _f_ of a node _v_, if both are retrieved during the search under a given \(\alpha\), the absolute difference between their Pareto angles, i.e., \(|\phi(v,e)-\phi(v,f)|\), should be constrained in a scope. Specifically, when computing the active ranges of a node’s candidate neighbors, ACAR employs different strategies for candidates in the first Pareto-frontier layer and those in the remaining layers, as shown in Algorithm 2. This is because nodes in the first layer are more likely to lie on the exact Pareto frontier, and thus require more precise active range computation. _(1) The First Layer_. In DEG, the first traversed node is assigned an active range of \[0,1\] simply because the neighbor set _NS_ is initially empty, which is clearly inaccurate. More importantly, the active range computation for nodes in the remaining layers depends on the active ranges of nodes in the first layer, making the accuracy of the first-layer active ranges crucial. To address this, ACAR employs a bidirectional two-stage scan over the first-layer candidate neighbors to compute more accurate active ranges. Specifically, in the first- stage scan, ACAR traverses the first-layer candidate neighbors in forward order to obtain the most reliable active ranges of the final retained node in _NS_ (line 4). After completing the forward scan, we perform a reverse scan with the same pruning operations (line 5), refining the active ranges of the first-layer neighbors. _(2) The Remaining Layers_. Since the proportion of candidate neighbors in the first layer is relatively small (only 4.53% on the OI dataset), the majority of the computational cost during the AR computation is incurred by computing the active ranges of candidate neighbors in the remaining layers. When computing the active ranges of each neighbor, DEG compares it with all nodes currently retained in _NS_, which leads to substantial computational overhead. ## 5 CONNECTIVITY-LOSS-DRIVEN INCREMENTAL PARETO FRONTIER REPAIR

As discussed in Section 2.3, applying single-vector repair methods for DVQ indices that incorporate Pareto frontiers is unable to simultaneously ensure update efficiency and retrieval effectiveness. To address this issue, we introduce a _connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair algorithm_ to maintain graph connectivity under deletions while avoiding unnecessary repair operations.

### 5.1 Observation & Intuition

For each affected node, reinsertion-based repair (RBR) methods perform Greedy Pareto Frontier Search from entry nodes to reconstruct its candidate neighbors. However, reinsertion incurs substantial redundant computations, resulting in inefficient updates.

**Observation.** To investigate the feasibility of incremental repair in Pareto-frontier-based indices under deletions, we measure the out-neighbor overlap ratio of affected nodes on three real-world datasets, as shown in Figure 7a. Specifically, we compute the overall overlap ratio of the out-neighbors for each affected node _v_, i.e., \(\frac{|N'_{out}(v)\cap N_{out}(v)|}{|N_{out}(v)|}\) , where _N<sub>out</sub>(v_) and \(N'_{out}(v)\) denote the out- neighbor sets before and after reinsertion, respectively. Furthermore, we analyze the overlap ratio across different layers of Pareto frontiers. Here, affected layers refer to layers that contain deleted nodes (i.e., layer 2). Low layers are defined as all layers below the lowest affected layer (i.e., layer 1), while high layers refer to the affected layers and all layers above them (i.e., layer 2 and layer 3), as illustrated in Figure 7b. We observe that 1) _the overall overlap ratio is at least 72%, indicating that most original neighbors remain effective after repair_, and 2) _87% of neighbors in low layers are preserved, whereas only 52% in high layers are retained._

**Intuition.** These observations provide strong support for incremental repair, which avoids the costly global search over all neighbors required by the reinsertion-based method. Observation 1) suggests<tbc>

<tbc>that most original neighbors of an affected node still belong to its approximate Pareto frontiers, enabling incremental repair during deletions. Furthermore, Observation 2) suggests that neighbor updates should be performed selectively across layers. Specifically, neighbors in low layers remain unchanged, while those in high layers need to be updated.

### 5.2 Pareto Frontier Repair Based on Connectivity Loss

We further analyze the distribution of deleted neighbors among affected nodes under a 1% deletion batch on the OpenImage index, with a maximum neighbor size of _R_=40. The results show that the number of deleted neighbors varies significantly across affected nodes (i.e., in-neighbors of deleted nodes), ranging from 1 to 20, indicating that the degree of connectivity loss induced by deletions differs substantially among affected nodes. We next provide a formal definition of connectivity loss.

Definition 2 (Connectivity Loss (CL)). _The connectivity loss of a node v measures the number of its lost out-neighbors, and its degree is defined as_

\(\mathrm{CL}(v)\unknown\frac{R-|N_{out}(v)|}{R},\) (3)

_where R denotes the maximum number of neighbors and N<sub>out</sub>(v_) _denotes the current out-neighbor set of v. It holds that_ \(\mathrm{CL}(v)\in[0,1]\).

Ideally, each node in the index maintains _R_ out-neighbors, resulting in no connectivity loss (CL=0). In practice, due to imperfect construction or deletions, nodes may suffer from connectivity loss. To this end, we categorize the degree of connectivity loss into three levels, mild, moderate, and severe. Specifically, for a node _v_, mild connectivity loss corresponds to \(\mathrm{CL}(v)\in[0,CL_1]\), moderate connectivity loss corresponds to \(\mathrm{CL}(v)\in(CL_1,CL_2]\), and severe connectivity loss corresponds to \(\mathrm{CL}(v)\in(CL_2,1]\), where _CL_<sub>1</sub> and _CL_<sub>2</sub> are the connectivity loss thresholds.

Given a deleted node, CA-PFR adaptively augments the candidate set C for each affected node \(v\in V_{affected}\), yielding a repaired candidate set \(\mathcal{C}'\). Therefore, the computational complexity for repairing an affected node _v_ is \(O(|\Delta C|)\), where \(\Delta C=\mathcal{C}'\backslash\mathcal{C}\) denotes

<tbc>the newly introduced candidate neighbors of _v_. Next, we analyze the size of \(|\Delta C|\) under the following three repair strategies of CA-PFR.

<u>_Historical-Pareto-Frontier Repair (Mild)_</u>. For each affected node \(v\in V_{affected}\), this strategy augments the original active out-neighbors in C with the active in-neighbors of _v_, resulting in \(|\Delta C|\approx|N_{in}(v)|\). Since the distances \(\delta_x(v,v')\) and \(\delta_y(v,v')\) are already stored in the corresponding in-neighbors \(v'\in N_{in}(v)\), the candidate set augmentation incurs no additional distance computations, i.e., _T<sub>mild</sub>_=0.

<u>_Affected-Layer Repair (Moderate)_</u>. In addition to the active in- neighbors _N<sub>in</sub>(v_), this repair strategy further adds the active out-neighbors of nodes in the affected layers to \(\mathcal{C}'\), yielding \(|\Delta C|\approx|N_{in}(v)|+n\cdot R\), where _n_ is the average number of nodes per layer, _R_ denotes the maximum out-degree, and \(n\le R\). Thus, the complexity for repairing each affected node _v_ is: \(T_{moderate}\approx O\left(n\cdot R\right)\).

<u>_Multi-Layer Repair (Severe)_</u>. This repair strategy not only includes the in-neighbors and the original active out-neighbors, but also incorporates all active out-neighbors of nodes in the high layers into \(\mathcal{C}'\), resulting in \(|\Delta C|\approx|N_{in}(v)|+h\cdot n\cdot R\), where _h_ is the number of the high layers, and \(h\cdot n\le R\). Therefore, the computational complexity of repairing each affected node _v_ is: \(T_{severe}\approx O\left(h\cdot n\cdot R\right)\).

Let _P_<sub>1</sub>, _P_<sub>2</sub>, and _P_<sub>3</sub> denote the probabilities of triggering the three repair strategies, respectively, satisfying _P_<sub>1</sub>+_P_<sub>2</sub>+_P_<sub>3</sub>=1. As a result, the computational complexity of CA-PFR is: \(T_{CA-PFR}=P_1\cdot T_{mild}+P_2\cdot T_{moderate}+P_3\cdot T_{severe}\). In practice, since severe repair is triggered infrequently, with probabilities satisfying \(P_1>P_2\gg P_3\), the expected complexity can be simplified as: \(\mathbb{E}[T_{CA-PFR}]=P'_2\cdot T_{moderate}\), where \(P'_2=\frac{P_2}{P_1+P_2}\).

**Evaluation Platform**. All experiments are conducted on a server with an Intel(R) CPU, 320 GB memory. The system runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS with GCC version 11.4.0.

**Workloads**. By default, we construct a DVQ index on 100% of each dataset for search and deletion experiments, and another index on 50% of each dataset for insertion experiments. **Metrics**. We measure search accuracy using Recall@_k_ (_k_=10 by default) and search efficiency using average query latency, while update (i.e., deletions and insertions) performance is evaluated using throughput (deletions/insertions per second).

## 6.7 Parameter Sensitivity

In ACTIVE , update performance is mainly affected by three parameters, namely the Pareto angle threshold \(\theta_{th}\) in ACAR, and the connectivity loss thresholds _CL_<sub>1</sub> and _CL_<sub>2</sub> in CA-PFR. We next study the impact of these parameters on update throughput and recall by varying them, and motivate the choice of the default settings.

**Pareto Angle Threshold.** In ACAR, a larger \(\theta_{th}\) allows each candidate node to be compared with more previously retained nodes, resulting in lower efficiency of the AR computation. To evaluate its impact, we conduct a sensitivity analysis on OI under 1% deletions and insertions by varying \(\theta_{th}\) among \(\pi/18\), \(\pi/6\), \(5\pi/18\), \(7\pi/18\), and \(\pi/2\), as shown in Figure 22. The results show that \(\theta_{th}=\pi/18\) achieves the highest throughput on both insertion and deletion, with only a small loss in Recall@10 relative to larger \(\theta_{th}\) values. Therefore, we set \(\theta_{th}\) to \(\pi/18\) by default.

## 6.8 Performance Gain

To evaluate the contribution of each core component to deletion performance, we start from RBR and progressively add the proposed components on three datasets under 0.1%, 1%, and 10% deletion batch sizes (see Figure 24), reporting normalized throughput relative<tbc>

<tbc>to RBR. Each component yields consistent speedups across batch sizes. Specifically, we first introduce the connectivity-loss-driven adaptive repair algorithm (+C.A.), which adaptively repairs affected nodes according to the degree of connectivity loss, achieving average speedups of 13.85\(\times\), 12.77\(\times\), and 11.34\(\times\) under the three batch sizes, respectively. We then further incorporate an asynchronously maintained reverse graph (+Async.), increasing the average speedups to 19.46\(\times\), 14.95\(\times\), and 12.27\(\times\), respectively, by avoiding scanning the entire graph topology. Finally, we introduce the angle-constrained AR computation algorithm (+A.C.), improving the average speedups to 25.76\(\times\), 25.50\(\times\), and 18.05\(\times\), respectively.

Notably, the asynchronously maintained reverse graph provides significant performance gains under the 0.1% batch size. Its main benefit is eliminating full graph scans, whereas the cost of in- memory access is relatively small.

## 7 RELATED WORK

**Hybrid Search.** To meet the demands of increasingly complex real-world applications, various hybrid search paradigms have been proposed, including filtered ANNS \[36, 45, 54, 64\] and multi- vector ANNS \[48\]. Filtered ANNS associates each object with both vector representations and structured attributes, supporting approximate nearest neighbor search under attribute constraints such as numerical ranges \[15, 25, 27, 37, 53, 58, 66\], temporal conditions \[52\], and categorical filters \[8, 17, 56\]. Multi-vector ANNS represents each object with multiple embeddings and jointly optimizes similarity across vector spaces \[6, 10, 14, 40, 41, 61\]. These paradigms extend traditional ANNS by incorporating structured or multi-view semantic information.

**Dual-Vector Query.** Existing dual-vector query approaches fall into two categories: preference-specific multi-index methods \[48, 63\] and preference-agnostic unified index methods \[61\]. The former fails to maintain high search accuracy under arbitrary query preferences, while the latter achieves a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off but does not support efficient updates.

**Chamfer-based Multi-Vector Retrieval (CMVR).** The similarity between objects in CMVR \[14\] is measured by CHAMFER\((Q,P)=\sum_{q_i\in Q}max_{p_j\in P}\langle q_i,p_j\rangle\), where _P_ and _Q_ denote the document and query vector sets, respectively. CMVR can capture finer-grained semantic information within a single feature than traditional _L_<sub>2</sub> or cosine distance measures applied to single-vector representations. This setting differs substantially from DVQ in both the retrieval task and the similarity measure, and therefore CMVR methods, such as MUVERA \[14\], cannot be used directly in DVQ tasks.

**Graph-based Index Updates.** In single-vector graph-based indices, dynamic updates \[18, 28, 57, 62\] have been extensively studied. Insertions are typically performed via incremental construction \[28, 47, 62\], and recent work such as ParlayANN \[31\] further accelerates this process through scalable and deterministic parallel batch insertion. Deletions are handled by either global reinsertion \[30, 60\] or local neighbor reconnection \[47, 62\].

## 8 CONCLUSION

We propose ACTIVE , a dynamic Pareto-frontier-based unified DVQ index that supports efficient updates while maintaining comparable retrieval quality under arbitrary query preferences. To accelerate index construction and insertions, we design an angle- constrained active range computation algorithm, ACAR, which reduces distance computations via Pareto-angle-based constraints. To support efficient updates, we further propose a connectivity-loss- driven adaptive repair algorithm (CA-PFR) that selects different repair strategies based on the connectivity loss of affected nodes. Experiments demonstrate that ACTIVE achieves a strong trade-off between retrieval quality and update throughput across datasets.

## A APPLICABILITY TO OTHER DUAL ATTRIBUTES

**Datasets with Additional Dual Attributes.** ACTIVE is not limited to image-text data, but supports arbitrary combinations of data types. To further examine the applicability of ACTIVE , we add two geo-tagged datasets, as shown in  3. The first is Regions (RS) \[1\], a multilingual geotagged social-media corpus collected from Twitter, where each text post is embedded using BERT \[13\]. The second is MP16-Pro (MP) \[24\], a geo-tagged image collection from Flickr, where each image is embedded into a 768-dimensional vector using DINOv2 ViT-B/14 \[35\]. We conduct both static search and dynamic update experiments on RS and MP.

**Static Search Performance.** The accuracy-efficiency trade-off results of ACTIVE , DEG, and MR on RS and MP are shown in Figure 27. Under the same search latency, the Recall@10 of ACTIVE is on average 0.83% and 0.32% lower than that of DEG on RS and MP, respectively. Meanwhile, ACTIVE substantially outperforms MR, improving Recall@10 by 33.10% on RS and by 15.17% on MP under the same latency. These results show that Pareto-frontier-based indices remain effective for text-coordinate and image-coordinate attribute pairs, and that ACTIVE preserves search quality close to DEG while clearly surpassing multi-index retrieval.

**Update Throughput.** We evaluate the update throughput of ACTIVE on RS and MP under 1% batch deletions and insertions, as shown in Figures 28 and 29. For deletions, ACTIVE consistently achieves higher throughput than both RBR and NRBR, improving the average deletion throughput by 13.78-23.88\(\times\) over RBR and 1.42-1.64\(\times\) over NRBR. For insertions, ACTIVE improves the average throughput by 1.31-1.48\(\times\) over DEG.

**Search Accuracy under Updates.** We further evaluate the search accuracy of ACTIVE under 1% batch deletions and insertions on RS and MP, as shown in Figures 30 and 31. For deletions, ACTIVE achieves Recall@10 comparable to that of RBR and 0.30%-0.58% higher than that of NRBR on average. For insertions, ACTIVE maintains Recall@10 comparable to that of DEG.

## C SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS OF THE PARETO ANGLE THRESHOLD \(\theta_{th}\)

To understand why HM is more sensitive to the Pareto angle threshold \(\theta_{th}\), we analyze the Pareto angle dispersion of its neighbors and the local neighborhood consistency between its two attribute spaces.

**Pareto Angle Dispersion**. We analyze the distribution of dual- attribute distances between each node _u_ and its neighbors, as shown in Figure 33. Specifically, for each node _u_, we collect the distance pairs \((\delta_x(u,v),\delta_y(u,v))\) for all its neighbors _v_ and aggregate them across all nodes to characterize the overall neighbor distribution of each dataset. HM exhibits a wider Pareto-angle interval containing 95% of the neighbor pairs, spanning \(55.5^\circ\), compared with \(31.0^\circ\) for OI and \(43.0^\circ\) for CM. To further quantify the dispersion of neighbors, we compute the average difference in Pareto angles among the neighbors of each node and average it across all nodes. Under the same maximum neighbor count _R_, HM exhibits a substantially larger mean angular difference of \(16.07^\circ\), compared with \(8.73^\circ\) for OI and \(10.38^\circ\) for CM. These results indicate that the neighbors of individual nodes in HM tend to be more widely spread in the Pareto angular space. Consequently, a small threshold may exclude more potentially useful pruning comparisons in HM, affecting neighbor selection quality and search performance.

**Local Neighborhood Consistency**. To understand the data properties underlying the differences in Pareto-angle distributions, we measure local neighborhood consistency directly from the attribute vectors, independently of the graph index. We uniformly sample 10,000 objects from each dataset and compute their exact nearest- neighbor rankings over the entire dataset, excluding the source object itself. For each sampled object, we identify its 100 nearest neighbors in attribute space _x_ and calculate their average distance- rank percentile in attribute space _y_. We then average these values across all sampled objects. As shown in  4, HM has a mean percentile of 49.99%, close to the expected percentile of approximately 50% for uniformly random candidates. In contrast, OI and CM have lower mean percentiles of 38.98% and 32.90%, respectively, indicating stronger local neighborhood consistency between the two attribute spaces. HM’s weaker consistency, together with its greater Pareto angular dispersion, helps explain why it is more sensitive to the threshold.
